$description: Tier 1 — core (brand-agnostic) primitive tokens. PRIVATE: never reference directly in app code. Brand-IDENTITY primitives (color.primaryRamp, color.saffron, color.navy, color.yellow) live in the active brand pack (packages/tokens/brands/<id>/brand.json) so the system can be white-labelled — see brands/README.md.

It was Material green #2E7D32, which sat 9 degrees and 6 L* from the logo green: two greens that close is a defect whichever token owns them. Brand-invariant (identical in Blue and Navy). Regenerate with: node build/brand-ramps.mjs then re-apply here. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs from the accentRamp anchor; do not hand-edit steps.

Step 950 added 2026-08-11 for UX4G parity (11 steps); derived from this ramp’s own 500 anchor, the 50-900 steps are untouched. neutral.$description: Neutral grey scale — matches UX4G/SAMAVESH Figma Neutral/* variables exactly. Endpoints renumbered 2026-08-11 to match UX4G: old 1000 -> 950, old 1100 -> 1000. Pure white (0) and pure black (1000) live ONLY on the neutral ramp — they are achromatic and cannot belong to a chromatic ramp. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

neutralDark.$description: NAVY BRAND neutral ramp (cooler Tailwind-family greys) — matches SAMAVESH Figma Palette/color/neutralScale/* in the Navy mode. Consumed via colorModes.navy on the neutral-derived semantic tokens. NOT a dark theme: the Navy brand renders on LIGHT surfaces, and the estate has no appearance axis at all (see apps/hub/src/app/globals.css). The key is still spelled `neutralDark` for the pre-2026-08-07 mode name; rename it with the ramp regeneration, not on its own. Endpoints renumbered 2026-08-11 to match UX4G: old 1000 -> 950, old 1100 -> 1000. Pure white (0) and pure black (1000) live ONLY on the neutral ramp — they are achromatic and cannot belong to a chromatic ramp. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

greenDbim.$description: Liberty Green — DBIM's SUCCESS status. DBIM functional palette (Table 1), group-independent — shared by all six DBIM conformance modes. CODE-ONLY. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

amberDbim.$description: Mustard Yellow — DBIM's WARNING status. ANCHORED AT 200, NOT 500: L* 84 is a TINT, and the rule this system keeps re-learning is that an anchor belongs at the rung its lightness says. It is also the one DBIM status that cannot carry white text anywhere near its published value (1.63:1), which is why its `bolder` fill takes dark ink. DBIM functional palette (Table 1), group-independent — shared by all six DBIM conformance modes. CODE-ONLY. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

redDbim.$description: Coral Red — DBIM's ERROR status. Anchored at 500 (L* 59) — the same rung our own #ec5042 used to occupy, and 4.53:1 is the same reason it had to leave. DBIM functional palette (Table 1), group-independent — shared by all six DBIM conformance modes. CODE-ONLY. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

infoDbim.$description: DBIM Blue — the INFORMATION status, and DBIM's hyperlink colour alongside the selected group's key colour. Anchored at 500 (L* 58), where gov-blue sits at L* 56. DBIM functional palette (Table 1), group-independent — shared by all six DBIM conformance modes. CODE-ONLY. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

neutralDbim.$description: DBIM's greys — PURE neutrals, R=G=B, chroma exactly 0, pinned at Linen #EBEAEA and the three published functional greys. Deliberately NOT tinted the way the blue and navy neutrals are: DBIM publishes flat greys, and tinting them would invent a colour DBIM never issued. CODE-ONLY. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

dbimInk.$description: Deep Earthy Brown — DBIM's body-text colour on a light background (Table 1). NOT black (#000000 is reserved for the State Emblem) and NOT a neutral step. 20.16:1 on white. CODE-ONLY. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs.

dbimPrimary.$description: DBIM's six primary colour groups, TRANSCRIBED from the DBIM ToolKit 'Colours' chapter (see reference/dbim-palette.json). Each group's five published shades appear VERBATIM at rungs 100/200/400/600/800 — shade 1 is the group's key colour — and the remaining six rungs are interpolated. Never re-derive these from an anchor: a conformance palette that has been re-derived is no longer a conformance palette. CODE-ONLY — the Figma exporter reads only `colorModes.navy`, so none of this can reach the library. GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs; do not hand-edit steps.

space.$description: Spacing ladder, VALUE-NAMED: `space/16` is 16px. Renamed from T-shirt labels on 2026-08-18. Two reasons, both measured. (1) A T-shirt ramp has no slot between two adjacent rungs, so every insertion forces a rename of everything above it — that happened twice in one day (inline gained 24, padding needed 6). A numeric ladder absorbs any step for free. (2) The Tier-2 families each mapped the SAME label to a DIFFERENT value — `l` was 16 in inline, 24 in stack, 20 in padding and 56 in section — which is inherited verbatim from UX4G 3.0 and is the single most confusing thing about the old scale. UX4G's own primitive ramp is numeric (space-1..16), so numbering here is MORE consistent with UX4G, not less. UX4G parity is unaffected: the --ux4g-* layer is emitted independently and never reads these names. 6px is new — UX4G ships it as space-3 and 400 padding properties in the Figma library needed it.

radius.$description: Radius ladder — VALUE-NAMED. The rung IS the pixel value, except `full`, a sentinel meaning fully rounded. Tier 1: hidden from publishing, banned in app code.

display.$description: The optical Display cut, for the 40-80px Display ramp. Noto Sans ships two cuts of one design: the text cut is drawn for reading at 12-24px, and at 80px its open spacing reads as loose. The Display cut tightens it. This is now genuinely LOADED (apps/hub root layout, weight 500) — for a long time it was named here and loaded nowhere, so it fell through to the text cut and the matching Figma variable could not resolve at all. LATIN ONLY: `Noto Sans Display` has no Devanagari subset and `Noto Sans Devanagari` has no Display cut, so a Hindi heading falls through to Noto Sans by design. In Figma the same cut is a STYLE of Noto Sans ("Display Medium"), not a family — see design.md.
display.$value: "Noto Sans Display", "Noto Sans", ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif

mono.$description: CODE AND TECHNICAL STRINGS ONLY — token names, CSS snippets, file paths in the design-system docs. NOT for numbers, amounts or reference numbers: those want `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` on Noto Sans, which aligns digits down a column while keeping them in the same typeface as the text beside them. Switching a data column to a monospace face is the clumsier fix and looks like a different design. The estate already does this correctly in the Aadhaar/PAN field, the charts, the SLA indicator and the shared DataTable. DELIBERATELY a system stack: `ui-monospace` resolves to the platform's own mono (SF Mono, Cascadia, Roboto Mono) — all well-drawn, all disambiguating 0/O and 1/l/I, and already on the device. A webfont here would download on every page to style sample code on a handful of documentation pages, which on a low-bandwidth government audience is not a trade worth making. IBM Plex Mono was set here briefly and reverted for that reason.
mono.$value: ui-monospace, "Cascadia Code", "Source Code Pro", Menlo, monospace

icon.$description: The ICON face — Material Symbols Rounded, the official SAMAVESH icon system. It is here for the same reason every other family is: a Material Symbols glyph is TEXT, not artwork, so its family is a typographic decision the design system owns rather than a constant three files happen to agree on. Before this token the name was a literal in `icons.css` (twice) and in all seven Figma `Icon/*` text styles, which is four places to change and no way to prove they still match. The stack is the family plus a generic, so a failed webfont falls back to a real face rather than to nothing; Figma takes only the first entry (`primaryFontFamily`), which is exactly the family name its picker resolves. NOT a Tier-2 role — bind `font/icon` from anything that renders.

size.$description: Legacy flat scale. New code should use font.role.* for the responsive role system.

role.$description: Two-surface responsive type role scale (Portal DS naming: hyphenated roles). Each size/lh/para carries mosje.type website/portal min+max bounds (min at 360px viewport, max at 1280px). The formatter emits --sa-type-ROLE-size/lh/para as clamp(min, fluid, max): Website in :root, Portal under data-surface=portal. $value is the Website desktop fallback.

tracking.$description: Letter-spacing (Portal DS naming). Website tracking is 0; Portal display tiers use negative tracking that scales with the fluid size. mosje.type website/portal min+max (px).

shadow.$description: Elevation ramp. none→xl is a 6-level superset of UX4G 3.0's 5-level l0…l4, and keeps the SAMAVESH convention of tinting toward ink (rgba(31,36,40,·)) rather than UX4G's flat black — tinted shadows read as depth instead of dirt on a light gov surface. sm/md fill the gap that previously jumped xs→lg. The ink is GENERATED by build/brand-ramps.mjs from neutral/800 — the body ink these are tinted toward — so it cannot drift from it again. Geometry stays authored here; only the rgb is derived.

motion.$description: Duration + easing primitives for transitions and animations.

outStrong.$description: Exponential ease-out. The built-in decelerate curve is too weak to read as intentional on a large surface: it leaves the gate slowly, which is the exact moment the reader is watching. This leaves fast and settles, so a panel reads as arriving under its own momentum rather than being played back at a fixed rate. Use it for anything the reader opens.

border.$description: Border widths. UX4G 3.0's exact values (border-none/thin/thick/thicker/thickest), bound by name so the two cannot drift — spec §8.1 'structural' rule.

opacity.$description: Opacity scale — thirteen steps, ONE ladder, derived from what the estate's translucent tokens use plus the two roles it will foreseeably need: 0 (transparent), 4 (hairline and faint lift on a dark surface), 8–48 in eights (the six wash and overlay tiers), 64 and 72 (disabled and secondary ink on a dark surface), 80 and 88 (pressed and hover fill of an inverse button), 100 (opaque). Rationalised 2026-09-04 from UX4G 3.0's fourteen steps plus ten estate one-offs: 5, 20, 25, 60, 75, 90 had zero consumers anywhere in the estate; 3, 10, 30, 45, 50, 70, 84, 92 each served one or two tokens and now sit on the ladder (3→4, 10→8, 30→32, 45→48, 50→48, 70→72, 84→80, 92→88). The UX4G parity stylesheet carries UX4G's own values as literals, so nothing UX4G publishes is lost; the divergence is recorded in docs/audit/2026-09-04-colour-system-audit-and-redesign.md §16. Consumers bind the Tier-2 `alpha/*` aliases, never this scale.

z.$description: Named stacking order. UX4G 3.0's z-index ladder verbatim — these numbers are Bootstrap's, which UX4G inherited and which third-party CSS in the estate already assumes, so diverging would put our modals under someone else's.

size.$description: One numeric size scale, VALUE-NAMED: `size/16` is 16px. Adopted from UX4G 3.0, whose 20 steps are carried at their exact rem values — the name needing no lookup is the thing worth copying, and it is what Tailwind and Spectrum do too. 22 and 44 are a SAMAVESH superset: our type scale already ships them and UX4G has no step there.

breakpoint.$description: Viewport anchors. These are not decoration: `clamp()` interpolates type between mobile and desktop, and Figma's Type modes sample the same curve at all three. The numbers were duplicated as literals in two build files until 2026-08-10 — this is now their one source.

laptop.$description: The third anchor, and the one the ladder was missing. Between tablet (768) and desktop (1280) sat a 512px void with no token in it — which is where iPad landscape, 11-13" laptops and every half-screen window on a 2K monitor live. Anything needing to change at 1024 had to hardcode it or round to one of the neighbours. Matches Tailwind's `lg`, so the token and the utility variant used across this estate finally agree. Viewport anchor. The ladder follows Material 3's window size classes, which are derived from measured device distribution rather than from one framework's grid: compact <600, medium 600-839, expanded 840-1199, large 1200-1599, extra-large >=1600. UX4G publishes the two content widths but no breakpoints at all, so there is nothing to diverge FROM here; where its guidance and interface quality met, quality won, per .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. Recorded in docs/guidelines/README.md.

desktopXl.$description: Where the content cap widens from `container/content` (1200) to `container/contentXl` (1320). 1768 -> 1600 -> 1440 over 2026-08-24, each step decided by measuring the page rather than by citing a ladder. 1768 was abandoned because a 1728-wide viewport carried 264px of margin each side against 1768's own 224px — margins NARROWING as the screen grew. 1600 (Material 3's extra-large window class) was then abandoned because it left the ladder's WEAKEST POINT sitting on its most common viewport: at 1536 — 1920 at 125% Windows scaling, the single most common desktop width — content held only 75% of the screen, worse than at 1280 (90%) and worse than at 1600 (78%). 1440 fixes the range that carries the most users: 1440 goes 80% -> 88%, 1512 76% -> 84%, 1536 75% -> 83%. Nothing at 1600 and above changes. THE FLOOR THAT WAS DROPPED, deliberately: earlier notes held that 1440 must stay on the 1200 cap because UX4G says '1200px desktop'. UX4G publishes no breakpoints at all, so it never fixed where desktop ends; and `.claude/rules/standards-precedence.md` puts interface quality above it, which is the whole point of that rule. Recorded as divergence #6 in docs/guidelines/README.md. It also makes the code agree with the Handoff, whose Home frame draws a 1320 container on a 1440 artboard — the frame was right and the note calling it wrong has been withdrawn. Not part of the type curve — `clamp()` still tops out at 1280, so this anchor resizes no glyph.

desktopWide.$description: The fifth anchor, where the cap widens a second time to `container/contentWide` (1440). Without it a 2560-wide monitor rendered a 1320 column between 620px margins — 48% of the screen given to nothing, which is the complaint that started this. One step is not enough for the range 1600-2560+: a single cap either starves the desktop or sprawls on the monitor. Stops at 1440 rather than continuing to grow because beyond that a 12-column grid starts costing more in eye travel than it returns in density. Viewport anchor. The ladder follows Material 3's window size classes, which are derived from measured device distribution rather than from one framework's grid: compact <600, medium 600-839, expanded 840-1199, large 1200-1599, extra-large >=1600. UX4G publishes the two content widths but no breakpoints at all, so there is nothing to diverge FROM here; where its guidance and interface quality met, quality won, per .claude/rules/standards-precedence.md. Recorded in docs/guidelines/README.md.
